procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated 28.11.2016 passed by the High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital in Appeal from Order No. 414 of 2010.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Uttarakhand at Nainital confirmed the judgment/award of the Tribunal solely considering the question of territorial jurisdiction. The High Court was approached under Section 173, M.V. Act, in an appeal filed by the appellant herein against the award of the Tribunal.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court was approached because the High Court confirmed the Tribunal's decision based solely on territorial jurisdiction, despite the Tribunal having erroneously decided other issues against the claimant even though it claimed it had no jurisdiction to do so. The Supreme Court disposed of the appeal, directing the parties to appear before the Tribunal and ordering the Tribunal to conclude the proceedings within a stipulated time.

directions: The parties shall appear before the Tribunal either in person or through counsel on 20.05.2024 and thereupon, the Tribunal shall conclude the proceedings within the above stipulated time.
The Registry shall forward copies of this judgment to all the parties.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the award of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal solely on the ground that the Tribunal lacked territorial jurisdiction, without considering the failure of justice caused by the Tribunal's procedural errors.

facts: A claimant filed a motor accident claim before a Tribunal in Kolkata. The accident and the claimant's residence were outside Kolkata's territorial jurisdiction, but the respondent insurance company had an office there.
The Tribunal, after taking evidence from both sides over a period of four years, dismissed the claim.

The Tribunal's reasoning was twofold: first, it found it lacked territorial jurisdiction. Second, based solely on this negative finding on jurisdiction, it decided all other six issues (concerning the merits of the accident claim) against the claimant without any examination or discussion of the evidence.
The High Court upheld the Tribunal's decision, confining its own review only to the question of territorial jurisdiction and ignoring the Tribunal's procedural error in deciding the other issues.
law: A distinction exists between a lack of territorial jurisdiction and a lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. An award from a Tribunal that lacks territorial jurisdiction is not a nullity.
The Motor Vehicles Act is a benevolent legislation, and procedural errors that defeat its purpose should be corrected.
The legal maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’ applies, meaning an act of the court shall not prejudice any party. A claimant should not be made to suffer for a mistake committed by the Tribunal.
An objection to territorial jurisdiction should not be a reason to set aside a decision unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.
application: The Supreme Court identified a "great illegality or error" committed by the Tribunal. The error was not just in finding it lacked jurisdiction, but in proceeding to decide all other substantive issues against the claimant without considering their merits.

This procedural error caused a significant "failure of justice." A simple dismissal for lack of jurisdiction would have allowed the claimant to file a new case in the correct court. However, by ruling against the claimant on all other issues, the Tribunal's award effectively became a final judgment on the merits, rendering the claimant remediless.

The Supreme Court heavily criticized the High Court for failing to notice this error. The High Court was wrong to confine its analysis solely to the territorial jurisdiction question while overlooking the prejudice and injustice caused by the Tribunal's flawed procedure.

The Court reasoned that since the Tribunal had already taken evidence on all issues, it should have pronounced findings on all of them based on merits, rather than dismissing them as a consequence of the jurisdictional finding. This would have allowed for a complete review by the appellate court.
Applying the maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’, the Court held that the claimant could not be penalized for the Tribunal's mistake.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the High Court's decision, holding that it was not justified in setting aside the award solely on the ground of territorial jurisdiction. The High Court erred by failing to consider the grave procedural illegality committed by the Tribunal—namely, deciding all substantive issues against the claimant without a merits-based examination. This error resulted in a clear failure of justice by rendering the claimant remediless, and therefore, the matter was remanded back to the Tribunal for a decision on the merits.

issue.issue_text: Whether the Claims Tribunal committed a procedural illegality by deciding all substantive issues against the claimant without an examination on merits, after having concluded that it lacked territorial jurisdiction.

facts: The Claims Tribunal, after hearing the case for approximately four years, concluded that it lacked the territorial jurisdiction to entertain the claim petition.
After making this determination, the Tribunal did not simply dismiss the case on that preliminary ground.
Instead, the Tribunal proceeded to decide all the other substantive issues (Nos. 1-4, 6, and 7) against the claimant and in favour of the opposite parties.
Crucially, the Tribunal did this while explicitly stating that it had "no occasion to examine the other issues on merits."
The High Court later upheld the dismissal, focusing only on the territorial jurisdiction issue and overlooking the Tribunal's error in deciding the other issues.
law: The Supreme Court applied the legal maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’, which means that an act of the court shall prejudice no one.
application: The Supreme Court identified the Tribunal's action as a "great illegality or error" that resulted in a "failure of justice."

The Court reasoned that a simple dismissal for lack of jurisdiction would have allowed the claimant to file a new claim in the correct tribunal. However, by also ruling against the claimant on all substantive issues, the Tribunal's decision became binding and effectively rendered the claimant "remediless."
The Court found it contradictory and prejudicial for the Tribunal to decide substantive issues against the claimant while simultaneously admitting it was not examining them on their merits.
Applying the maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’, the Court held that the claimant should not be made to suffer for the mistake committed by the Tribunal.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the Claims Tribunal committed a clear procedural illegality. By deciding the substantive issues against the claimant without a merits-based examination after it had already found it lacked jurisdiction, the Tribunal caused great prejudice and a failure of justice. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the Tribunal's findings on the substantive issues.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in setting aside the award of the Motor Accident Claims Tribunal solely on the ground that the Tribunal lacked territorial jurisdiction, without considering the failure of justice caused by the Tribunal's procedural errors.
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in upholding the dismissal of the claim petition solely on the ground of lack of territorial jurisdiction.
The High Court should have considered the significant procedural errors committed by the Tribunal and the resulting failure of justice, rather than limiting its review to the jurisdictional question.
respondent_arguments: The High Court's decision was correct as the Claims Tribunal fundamentally lacked the territorial jurisdiction to hear the case.
The lack of territorial jurisdiction is a preliminary and fatal defect, making it unnecessary to consider other aspects of the case.
The respondents had consistently raised the objection regarding the lack of territorial jurisdiction from the beginning of the proceedings.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the Claims Tribunal committed a procedural illegality by deciding all substantive issues against the claimant without an examination on merits, after having concluded that it lacked territorial jurisdiction.
appellant_arguments: The Claims Tribunal committed a procedural illegality by proceeding to decide substantive issues against the claimant after it had already determined that it lacked territorial jurisdiction.
Once the Tribunal concluded it had no jurisdiction, it should have returned the claim for presentation to the proper forum instead of adjudicating on the merits.
respondent_arguments: The primary finding of the Tribunal regarding the lack of territorial jurisdiction was correct and sufficient to dispose of the claim.
Any subsequent findings on substantive issues by the Tribunal are irrelevant because the case was rightly dismissed on jurisdictional grounds.

cases.case_name: Mantoo Sarkar v. Oriental Insurance Company Ltd.
cases.principle: The provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure are applicable to proceedings before the Motor Accidents Claims Tribunal, subject to any specific rules to the contrary.
A defect of jurisdiction can be corrected by a court only if it has occasioned a failure of justice.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In an appeal against an award where a claim for compensation was dismissed on the preliminary ground of territorial jurisdiction, the appellate court must consider not only the correctness of the jurisdictional finding but also whether it has occasioned a failure of justice. The court is bound to take into consideration any illegality resulting in a failure of justice, even if not specifically pleaded, due to the benevolent nature of the compensation provisions.
obiter: The principles laid down in the Code of Civil Procedure may be held to be applicable in a case of this nature.

The legislative intention is that all possible care should be taken to ensure that the time, energy and labour spent by a Court did not go in vain unless there has been a consequent failure of justice.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: A great illegality or error was committed by the Tribunal when, after finding it lacked territorial jurisdiction, it proceeded to decide the remaining six substantive issues against the claimant without any examination on the merits. This action caused a failure of justice by rendering the claimant remediless, as the findings would be binding. This mistake by the Tribunal cannot be allowed to prejudice the claimant, in line with the maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’ (an act of the court shall prejudice no one).
legal_tests_applied: Under Section 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an objection to territorial jurisdiction cannot be entertained by an Appellate or Revisional Court unless the objection was taken at the earliest opportunity and "unless there has been a consequent failure of justice."

A distinction is made between a lack of territorial jurisdiction, which does not automatically render a judgment a nullity, and an inherent lack of jurisdiction over the subject matter, which would make a judgment a nullity.
The maxim ‘Actus Curiae neminem gravabit’ is applied, meaning no party shall be made to suffer for a mistake of a Court.
policy_considerations: The legislative intention behind Section 21, CPC is that "all possible care should be taken to ensure that the time, energy and labour spent by a Court did not go in vain unless there has been a consequent failure of justice."

The provisions for granting compensation under Section 166 of the Motor Vehicles Act are benevolent in nature, and if an illegality resulting in a failure of justice is discernible, the Court is bound to consider it even without a specific pleading.
A remand after a long passage of time may be a futility, as witnesses may become unavailable for various reasons, including death, making it necessary to correct the Tribunal's error directly.
